1.pericope_label: Ahaz begins to reign, walks in the ways of the kings of Israel and burns his children

schools.summary: Gill says only that these verses are much the same as the parallel in Kings, with one difference of wording there.

Ellicott finds the opening verse identical with its parallel, but records that the Greek, Syriac and Arabic read twenty-five years rather than twenty, and that some manuscripts and the Syriac add the words his God to the divine name as Kings does; he adds that the Assyrian monuments call this king Yahuhazi, that is Jehoahaz, of which Ahaz may be a familiar abridgement on the pattern by which Jonathan becomes Nathan. On the molten images he explains that they were made for the Baals, the different aspects of the Canaanite god, and that the clause is the chronicler’s own addition explaining the one before it, the way of the kings of Israel having been the state recognition of Baal worship side by side with that of Jehovah — while allowing Thenius’s alternative that this clause and the next may simply have fallen out of the text of Kings. On the valley he traces a word into the New Testament: the incense went to Moloch, god of Ammon, for whom Solomon had built a high place still standing, and the valley’s name, spelt as one word and with modified vowels, later became the appellation of hell, so used in the Targums and the Talmud and reaching the New Testament in a Graecised form from which the Latin name descends. On the burning of the children he notes that Kings says rather that Ahaz made his own son pass through the fire, that the chronicler has reached burning by transposing two Hebrew letters, and that the plural is a generalised expression; Thenius accuses the chronicler of exaggerating, but Ellicott answers that this use of the plural is one of the marks of his style. Keil and Delitzsch reserve their comment for the war that follows, referring its course to their treatment of the parallel and observing only that the chronicler brings the two main battles prominently forward.

Clarke does not resolve the king’s age, referring the difficulties of the chronology to his note on the parallel passage. On the burning of the children he sets beside the verse a remarkable addition in the Chaldee, which has the Word of the Lord snatch Hezekiah from among the children Ahaz burnt, because the three righteous men Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah were to proceed from him and were themselves to be delivered from a burning furnace for the sake of the great and glorious Name; the passage then numbers five escapes from fire — Abram cast in by Nimrod for refusing the idols, Tamar in the house of judgment of Judah, Hezekiah thrown by his father into the valley on the altars of Tophet, the three men in the furnace of Nebuchadnezzar, and Joshua the son of Josedek, who escaped for his righteousness where two others cast in with him were consumed.

5.pericope_label: Ahaz delivered to Syria and to Israel; great slaughter in Judah and captives carried to Samaria

schools.summary: Gill gives three grounds for the text calling the Lord the God of such a king: God was his of right, having dominion over him and deserving his worship; his by the national covenant with the people Ahaz was king of; and his by Ahaz’s own hypocritical profession, while he forsook the true worship. He accounts for the ease of the captivity, that after such a slaughter of the men the rest were intimidated; and remembering the third verse, he observes that the king’s son killed in the battle must then have escaped being burnt in the valley of Hinnom, or was only made to pass through the fire there.

Ellicott explains the divergence from Kings by the writer’s purpose: the chronicler means not so much to describe a campaign as to select the events that most conspicuously illustrate God’s chastisement of an apostate king, so that the historical is subordinated to the didactic — not history for its own sake but history teaching by example — while adding that this does not make the events doubtful, Thenius having characterised the whole section as thoroughly historical. So instead of the joint attempt on Jerusalem and the seizure of the southern port, the chronicler prefers two severe defeats in the open field before the retreat behind the walls, after which the confederates converged on the capital, the panic at their coming being finely depicted by Isaiah and their attempt proving ineffectual as that prophet had foretold. He treats both casualty totals as round numbers, observes that the figure would mean about a third of the Jewish host fell, and produces a corroboration no one else has: Sennacherib boasts of taking forty-six strong cities of Judah and carrying off two hundred thousand one hundred and fifty captives, so the figure here is confirmed from a foreign and wholly unrelated source. Keil and Delitzsch defend the same figures against named critics who called them the exaggerations of a wonder-loving chronicler, holding that Isaiah shows the allied kings purposed to annihilate Judah outright and that the Ephraimites always acted with extreme cruelty in war. Both note that the word brethren is used with emphasis, marking the cruelty of carrying off the defenceless women and children of one’s own kin; and both identify the three men killed beside the king as a prince of the royal house rather than a son of Ahaz, who so early could not have had a son old enough to bear arms, a palace official rather than a temple one, and the second from the king, his first minister. Ellicott says why the three are named at all, their intimate connection with Ahaz being the point, since the blow that struck them struck the king whose punishment is described; and he glosses in one day as one great engagement, the word day bearing among Hebrews and Arabs the force of a day of battle.

Clarke doubts the casualty figures outright: very probably there is a mistake, since it is hardly possible that a hundred and twenty thousand men were slain in one day — though he concedes that all the versions and manuscripts agree in it. Wesley puts the question about the divine name more sharply than Gill, that God was his God not by the special relation, which Ahaz had renounced, but by sovereign dominion, for God did not forfeit his right by Ahaz denying it.

9.pericope_label: Oded the prophet confronts the returning host, and the Ephraimite chiefs send the captives home clothed and fed

schools.summary: Gill is careful to say this Oded is not the Oded of Asa’s day, and reads the enslaving of the captives as contrary to the law.

Ellicott notes that the whole section is peculiar to the chronicler, who told it his own way, so that the words of the prophet and the chiefs may be mainly his, though there is no ground for doubting its general truth; of Oded nothing further is known, and he was a prophet of Jehovah, not of the Baals. What Ellicott finds remarkable is a silence: neither here nor in the parallel is any mention of Hosea, who must have been active at this epoch in the northern kingdom. He puts the prophet’s argument bluntly — the victory was owed to the punitive wrath of Jehovah, not to their own valour or intrinsic superiority, which they ought to have considered and shown compassion to the victims of divine displeasure, whereas they gave full rein to the savage dictates of furious hatred — and reads the question either as whether they are wholly guiltless or whether they are the only guiltless people, the reference perhaps being to the calves of Bethel and Dan, noting also that the law forbids the permanent enslaving of Israelites by Israelites. He asks why the chronicler lingers on the kindness and answers three ways: the writer dwells with manifest pleasure on the mercy of these repentant foes, and may have meant a lesson for the Samaritans of his own age, whose hostility so damaged the restored exiles and who by rabbinic tradition tried to prejudice Alexander the Great against Jerusalem; some have supposed our Lord had this passage in mind in the parable of the good Samaritan, the coincidences being at any rate curious; and he defends the episode by symmetry, an Ephraimite prophet interposing between Ephraimites and their Judaean captives being precisely parallel to the Judaean prophet Shemaiah interposing between his people and the ten tribes, so that granting the truth of the one leaves no ground for suspecting the other. Keil and Delitzsch reach for Hosea to the contrary purpose, as proof that a true prophet could be found in Samaria at all, not of the Jahve there worshipped in the calf images but of the true God, and compare Oded’s going to meet the army with Azariah meeting Asa. They have the prophet quicken the conscience first and only then demand, the butchery being already a sin crying to heaven and the carrying off of women and children filling up its measure, so that the question whether there are not sins with them, even with them, asserts in a lively way what is not in doubt; and they call the description of the captives’ relief picturesque.

Clarke declines to comment on the prophet’s speech and then gives the chapter’s strongest verdict: to this beautiful speech nothing can be added by the best comment, it being simple, humane, pious and overwhelmingly convincing, and no wonder it produced the effect recorded. That the Ephraimite chiefs had much humanity the fifteenth verse proves, for they did not barely dismiss these unfortunate captives but took the very spoil their army had brought away, and clothed, fed, shod and anointed them, set the feeblest upon asses and escorted them safely to Jericho; we can scarcely find a parallel to it, he concludes, in the universal history of the wars savage man has carried on against his fellows from the foundation of the world. Wesley finds in the surrender of the captives a more truly heroic bravery than the taking of them, since it is true honour to yield to reason and religion even in spite of interest.

16.pericope_label: Ahaz appeals to Assyria while Edom and the Philistines invade; Tilgath-pilneser distresses and does not strengthen him

schools.summary: Gill takes the plural kings of Assyria literally, of Tiglath-pileser and his son, noting that the Greek, Latin, Syriac and Targum read the singular. He has the Philistines fall first on the cities nearest them and press as far as the south, in revenge for what Uzziah had done. On the title king of Israel he offers three grounds at once — that Ahaz walked in the ways of those kings, that he ruled two of the tribes, and that of right he was king over all Israel as David and Solomon had been — while noting that the Greek, Latin, Syriac and Targum read Judah; and he takes the making of Judah naked as a stripping of treasure, of strongholds, and above all of religion and the divine protection.

Keil and Delitzsch alone make the plural carry a charge: it is rhetorical, since the chronicler himself shows later that only one king was approached, and by it the thought is expressed that Ahaz, instead of seeking the help of his own God which the prophet had promised, turned to the kings of a world-power hostile to the kingdom of God, from whom he could get no real help. They have the Edomites, subdued lately by Amaziah and Uzziah and freed by Rezin, seize the moment for vengeance, and the Philistines use the pressure of Syrians and Ephraimites not merely to shake off their yoke but to enlarge their territory. They deny that the title king of Israel refers to Ahaz walking in those kings’ ways and make it ironical instead, his government having been the bitterest satire upon the name of a king of Israel, that is of the people of God. Ellicott calls the plural a generalised expression of the kind the chronicler uses elsewhere, sets out the ground the Philistines took and reads their occupation as permanent rather than a raid, and rejects the irony most commentators see in the title, holding that the southern kingdom simply was Israel in the chronicler’s idea, however much more important the northern was politically, as the cedar of Lebanon beside the blackthorn beside it. Both agree the verb rendered made Judah naked means that Ahaz behaved loosely in Judah rather than that he made Judah loose, the construction forbidding the latter. Ellicott describes what the Assyrian wanted: glad of a pretext for interference in the west, the usurper was bent on extending his empire, and once Syria and Israel lay at his feet he required an unequivocal acknowledgement of vassalage, distressing Ahaz by reducing the kingdom to a dependency and stripping the treasure sent as the price of that ruinous help; and he quotes a modern historian that the principle of that monarchy was plunder and its kings had no regard to their vassals.

Clarke treats the singular as the true text, the versions and the parallel place having it, and says simply that the Assyrian did Ahaz no ultimate service. Wesley keeps the plural but lowers it to princes, called kings in a looser sense; he takes the nakedness as stripping of treasure, frontier towns, religion and the divine protection, which he calls their only firm security; and he alone explains why the help was no help, the expression being most emphatical, for though Tiglath weakened the Syrian, who, troublesome neighbour though he was, had served Judah as a kind of bulwark, his removal only smoothed the way for a far more dangerous enemy, as appeared in the very next reign.

22.pericope_label: Ahaz sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, cuts up the temple vessels and shuts its doors, and dies unburied with the kings

schools.summary: Gill first takes the sacrificing as Ahaz’s own folly, imagining the gods of Damascus might do him no more hurt, as it is said of the Indians that they worship the devil so that he may not hurt them, which he calls monstrous stupidity in a king of Judah; but he then proposes a construction saving the writer, that the meaning may rather be the gods of those who smote him, the men of Damascus, since the Spirit of God would never ascribe the smiting to idols, however Ahaz might. He also reads the increase of idolatry as imitation of what Ahaz had seen at Damascus.

Ellicott puts the question others avoid, whether the chronicler himself believed the gods of Aram had any real existence; he thinks it certain the Israelites of Ahaz’s day commonly did, and notes that while the latter half of Isaiah asserts the nothingness of false gods, another opinion also ran, which Paul repeats and Milton adopted, that what the heathen sacrifice they sacrifice to demons. He reads the closing clause as pointed, those very gods being to Ahaz a stumbling, and to all Israel; glosses the cutting of the vessels as trimming off their metal ornaments; notes that the shutting of the doors is absent from Kings and insists it was the sanctuary doors and not the great court’s, so that all rites confined to the Holy Place were suspended; suggests the sacrilege was committed in collecting anything of value for the rapacious Assyrian; makes the grammar carry the verdict on the man, the subject being emphatically repeated so that it reads he, king Ahaz, the notorious apostate, who having been sorely chastised sinned yet more; and answers Thenius on the burial clause, which Thenius supposed founded on mistake or on zeal for the Law, with the obvious alternative, why not upon a written authority. Keil and Delitzsch fight over a participle, insisting against Bertheau that it must not be rendered as a pluperfect, since Ahaz sought the Syrian gods’ help not after the Syrians had defeated him but while they were defeating him, during the war and not after it. They say he was not content with strange gods but laid hands on the vessels and suppressed the worship, cautioning that the gathering and the word all are rhetorical, the cutting meaning by the parallel account the mutilating of the wrought vessels of the court and the taking down of the brazen sea from its oxen onto a stone pavement; and on the burial they find a deliberate choice of words, that he was buried in the city, in Jerusalem, but not in the graves of the kings, the phrasing seeming selected to intimate that one who had not walked like his ancestor David was not laid beside him.

Clarke quotes a commentator surprised at the text on the ground that Scripture everywhere represents heathen idols as nothing and vanity, incapable of good or hurt, so that an inspired author cannot have written that they smote Ahaz; the difficulty is avoided by following the older Hebrew copies behind the Greek, which make the words Ahaz’s own — I will seek to the gods of Damascus which have smitten me — a turn the Syriac and Arabic share. He notes that the temple doors stayed shut until the next reign, and thinks the burial clause of little importance, taking it as this writer’s common habit of putting Israel for Judah, considering them one people from one stock. Wesley is the most violent of the five on the man himself: that monster and reproach of mankind, that unteachable and incorrigible prince, whom even grievous afflictions made worse where they commonly make men better, and whose name deserves to be remembered and detested for ever.
